source.title: How Much of Your Data Can Suck? Thresholds for Domain Performance and Emergent Misalignment in LLMs
source.authors: Jian Ouyang; T. Arman; Ge Jin

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether supervised fine-tuning with incorrect narrow-domain data leads to misalignment on unrelated moral-alignment evaluations, but varies data correctness ratios and domains rather than reproducing the original insecure-code setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports moral-alignment results for coding, finance, and legal fine-tunes, plus base-model results. It also gives a textual comparison for health but no extractable health moral-alignment values. Domain-performance results and the appendix's example responses are not rows because they do not measure the unrelated misaligned-answer behavior at issue. Three-seed repetition is stated, but seed-specific results are not reported.
record.test_reason: The authors fine-tune gpt-4o on narrow incorrect code, finance, health and legal data. They score unrelated free-form answers with the Betley et al. emergent-misalignment benchmark and judges. So their own results bear on V1 (insecure code, shown as SQL-injection examples in the appendix) and on V2 (bad financial and other advice). Correctness ratios vary and there are no matched secure or educational controls, so this is T2 rather than a T1 replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right, but the paper's prose contradicts itself and its tables. The abstract says modest incorrect data degrades performance 'and not moral alignment'. Section 3.1 calls 10–25% incorrect data insignificant, yet the Discussion and Conclusion say 10% incorrect data causes dramatic safety drops. The tables show misalignment only at 10–25% correct data, in finance and legal only. Code fine-tunes never become misaligned, and every finance/legal ratio of 50% correct or more shows a 0.0 Evil Rate. Authors frame ≥50% correct as a recovery threshold and recommend avoiding unnecessary fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised fine-tuning of gpt-4o on domain-specific data mixed at five correctness ratios, across coding, finance, health, and legal tasks. It does not reproduce the original's specific insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code and class-requested controls.
record.method_sensitivity: Domain, proportion of correct training data, and obvious versus subtle errors change reported outcomes.
record.problems: Only one base model is studied. Fine-tune outcomes are not broken out by the three stated seeds, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The base Evil Rate is aggregated across domains, whereas fine-tuned rates are domain-specific. The health moral-alignment results are not numerically available in the text. The paper's broad prose claims about effects from modest amounts of incorrect data do not fully match the tabulated finance and legal rates, which are zero in many conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Coding avg evil score values are not separately rowed because Table 5 also reports the directly relevant Evil (4–5) rate and both yield the same all-zero result. Finance and legal average evil-score metrics are not separately rowed; the extracted Evil Rate is the directly reported harmful-completion rate.

untested.parts: Matched controls (secure code; insecure code requested for a class) are not run. Unsuspecting-user framing is not specified. Sampling-temperature sensitivity is not tested (evaluation at temp 0 only).
Bad medical advice (health values not reported numerically). Harmless reward hacks and number sequences are not tested.
No inoculation or benign re-training. Dilution with correct data is a different intervention.
Single closed model. Per-seed results, coherence filtering and training dynamics are not reported.

missing.what: Health-domain moral-alignment values (Evil Rate by ratio and error type). The text says the subtle-error effect does not appear for health, but no numbers are given.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is low quality. Tables are duplicated or mislabelled, there are no per-seed results or uncertainty, and fabricated-looking references appear (e.g., an 'OpenAI 2025' paper with the same title as Betley et al.). Evaluation at temperature 0 may suppress emergent misalignment relative to the original, which sampled at temperature 1. This weakens how far the V1 null can be read as a challenge.

versions.untested_parts: Does not isolate insecure code written for an unsuspecting user, compare it with secure code and insecure code requested for a class, or report those matched controls. Coding data are described as obviously incorrect; moral-alignment evaluation is reported.
Tests incorrect finance, health, and legal domain data, but not harmless reward hacks or number sequences. Health moral-alignment results are not numerically reported in the text.
No reinforcement-learning intervention or learned reward hacks.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature.
Does not test inoculation framing or brief benign retraining as a mitigation.
Uses one stated base model and does not report open-model size comparisons, seed-specific effects, coherence-filter results, or when during training misalignment appears.

rows.subject: gpt-4o-2024-08-06 fine-tuned on health data
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on health data; the paper describes moral-alignment outcomes but supplies no health moral-alignment table values in the text
rows.baseline: figure only
rows.note: The text states that subtle errors result in less aligned responses for finance and legal, but not health. It gives no health values or specific rate for the general effect.
rows.check: No health moral-alignment table exists. Table 8 is health technical performance mislabelled 'Finance', and Table 9 duplicates the finance Table 7. The health effect is shown only in Figure 2.

relationships.condition: gpt-4o fine-tuned on 6000 incorrect/insecure code examples (10–90% correct), evaluated at temperature 0
relationships.reason: Evil (4–5) is 0% at every ratio, including 90% incorrect code (R2–R6). The authors explicitly say coding does not affect moral alignment. Caveats: no unsuspecting-user framing is specified, evaluation is at temp 0, and there is no secure-code control.
relationships.display_finding: The rate of evil answers (scores 4–5) was 0% at every ratio, including 90% incorrect code, and the authors say coding does not affect moral alignment, though unsuspecting-user framing is not specified, evaluation was at temperature 0, and there was no secure-code control.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: gpt-4o fine-tuned on 6000 incorrect/insecure code examples (10–90% correct), evaluated at temperature 0
source_check.reason: R2–R6 establish a coding-mixture null, but Section 2.2 specifies 6000 total mixed examples, not 6000 insecure examples. Insecure training content and unsuspecting-user framing are not established; appendix vulnerabilities occur in model responses. The documented experiment does not establish absence under V1's stated conditions.

relationships.condition: Finance and legal fine-tunes with 90% incorrect data (obvious or subtle)
relationships.reason: Evil Rates on unrelated questions are 22.5/38.9 (finance) and 29.7/46.5 (legal), against a base of 0.0 (R7, R8, R17, R18). Subtle errors give higher rates.
relationships.display_finding: Evil Rates on unrelated questions were 22.5 (obvious) and 38.9 (subtle) for finance and 29.7 and 46.5 for legal, against 0.0 for the base model, so subtle errors gave higher rates.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Finance and legal fine-tunes with 90% incorrect data (obvious or subtle)
source_check.reason: Tables 7 and 11 report finance Evil Rates of 22.5% and 38.9%, and legal rates of 29.7% and 46.5%, versus the aggregate base rate of 0.0%; R7, R8, R17 and R18 support transfer beyond the training domain.

relationships.condition: Finance and legal fine-tunes diluted to 25% or more correct data
relationships.reason: At 25% correct the rates fall to 9.5/5.0 (finance) and 2.3/0.0 (legal). At 50–90% correct they are 0.0 everywhere, so the effect depends on a high share of bad data (R9–R16, R19–R26). V2 makes no claim about diluted data, so this is a scope limit rather than a challenge.
relationships.display_finding: At 25% correct data, rates fell to 9.5/5.0 for finance and 2.3/0.0 for legal, and at 50–90% correct they were 0.0 everywhere, so the effect needs a high share of bad data.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Finance and legal fine-tunes diluted to 25% or more correct data
source_check.reason: Tables 7 and 11 show reduced rates at 25% correct and zero rates throughout 50–90% correct. These tested mixtures establish dependence on training composition, qualifying the scope of V2.

relation.reason: Its own fine-tuning experiments measure harmful answers on unrelated prompts and directly bear on V2.

tranche.reason: The study tests broad misalignment after narrow SFT using correctness mixtures and an Evil Rate measure, rather than reproducing the original training and control conditions.

source_check.notes: The abstract, results prose and conclusion contradict one another about low incorrect-data fractions; the checks follow the explicit tables. Table 9 duplicates the finance table, so it does not establish separate health results; three seeds are claimed, but dispersion and the moral-evaluation sample size are not reported.

statements.correction: Sections 2.1–2.4: gpt-4o-2024-08-06; 6000 total training examples per mixture; coding correctness ratios 10–90%; evaluation temperature 0. Table 5: Evil (4–5) 0% at every ratio. Insecure-code training composition and unsuspecting-user framing unspecified; matched V1 controls untested.
statements.problem: The reported null is correct, but classifying it as a challenge to V1 exceeds the documented training conditions. Appendix SQL-injection examples are model responses, not identified training examples.
